title: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis
summary: Primary sclerosing cholangitis requires cholangiographic confirmation, exclusion of secondary causes, systematic evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease, and surveillance for hepatobiliary and colorectal malignancy. No drug has established disease-modifying benefit; management centers on complications, selected biliary intervention, and timely transplant referral.
seoDescription: Point-of-care review of primary sclerosing cholangitis diagnosis, cancer surveillance, biliary stricture management, IBD assessment, and transplant referral.
clinicalQuestion: How should clinicians diagnose, monitor, and manage complications and malignancy risk in primary sclerosing cholangitis?
keyTakeaways: Suspect PSC with cholestatic liver injury; MRCP is the preferred noninvasive cholangiographic test, while ERCP is generally reserved for unresolved diagnostic questions or therapeutic evaluation of a clinically relevant stricture. [11][21]
Assess every patient with PSC for concomitant IBD, including diagnostic colonoscopy when IBD is not already known; PSC is frequently associated with IBD, predominantly ulcerative colitis. [21]

There is no established disease-modifying pharmacotherapy for PSC; management prioritizes symptom control, treatment of biliary and cirrhotic complications, malignancy surveillance, clinical trials, and transplant referral when indicated. [13][19][21]

New or worsening jaundice, pruritus, cholangitis, biochemical deterioration, or a concerning stricture should trigger evaluation for obstruction and cholangiocarcinoma rather than attribution to PSC progression alone. [11][23]

Liver transplantation is appropriate for decompensated cirrhosis and may be considered for recurrent bacterial cholangitis, severe refractory pruritus or jaundice, high-grade biliary dysplasia, selected hepatocellular carcinoma, and carefully selected hilar cholangiocarcinoma. [16][21]

sections.heading: Confirm PSC and exclude mimics
sections.intro: The central diagnostic decision is whether cholangiographic abnormalities represent primary rather than secondary sclerosing cholangitis.
paragraphs: PSC should be considered with a cholestatic biochemical pattern, including elevated alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyltransferase, or bilirubin, with or without symptoms. The defining clinical framework combines cholestatic liver biochemistry with multifocal biliary stricturing on cholangiography. [12][21]

MRCP is generally the first cholangiographic study because it noninvasively evaluates intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts, including ducts proximal to severe stenoses. Reported MRCP sensitivity and specificity for PSC are 85% to 88% and 92% to 97%, respectively; subtle early disease can be missed, and cirrhosis can distort ducts and mimic PSC. [11]

ERCP is not a routine diagnostic substitute for MRCP because it is invasive, but it is appropriate when MRCP is nondiagnostic despite persistent clinical suspicion or when a stricture requires endoscopic assessment or therapy. ERCP also enables tissue-directed evaluation when malignancy is a concern. [11]
bullets: Review the clinical context for secondary sclerosing cholangitis, including infection, neoplasia, or other obstructive and inflammatory biliary disorders before assigning a primary diagnosis. [20]
Use liver biopsy selectively: sampled large-duct PSC can yield nonspecific portal inflammation and fibrosis, and classic duct-centered pathology may not be present in a limited specimen. [20]

Obtain a diagnostic colonoscopy to evaluate for occult IBD when it is not already established. Approximately 68% of patients with PSC have IBD in population-based data, most commonly ulcerative colitis. [21]

Look for intrahepatic and/or extrahepatic multifocal stricturing; assess alternative structural explanations. [11][12]

Evaluate for a clinically important stricture and cholangiocarcinoma rather than presuming uncomplicated PSC progression. [11][23]

sections.heading: Risk is driven by progressive biliary injury and malignancy
sections.intro: Prognosis is heterogeneous, but progressive liver disease and hepatobiliary malignancy determine major outcomes.
paragraphs: PSC is a chronic fibroinflammatory cholangiopathy that can progress to biliary cirrhosis, portal-hypertensive complications, and liver failure. A review of PSC natural history reported median transplant-free survival of approximately 15 years, although individual trajectories vary substantially. [13]

Cholangiocarcinoma is a defining competing risk. Published estimates in the supplied literature place lifetime cholangiocarcinoma risk at approximately 10% to 15%, although broader estimates of 9% to 31% have also been reported. [10][11] This variation underscores uncertainty in counseling an individual patient, but supports a low threshold to investigate a new obstructive or constitutional change.

Gallbladder cancer risk is also increased. Reported prevalence estimates range from 2.5% to 3.5%, with substantially higher estimates in some series; prognosis after gallbladder cancer diagnosis is poor. [23]
bullets: Do not use carbohydrate antigen 19-9 alone to diagnose or screen for cholangiocarcinoma: up to 33% of patients with PSC can have an elevated value without cholangiocarcinoma or another identified cause. [23]
When MRI/MRCP identifies a suspicious stricture or mass, CA 19-9 may complement imaging but should not replace diagnostic evaluation. [23]

Discuss early transplant-center involvement as complications emerge; transplantation offers excellent post-transplant outcomes, with generally greater than 85% five-year survival reported by AASLD educational material. [21]

sections.heading: Treat complications; do not overstate medical therapy
sections.intro: No pharmacologic treatment in the supplied evidence has established disease-modifying benefit in PSC.
paragraphs: Effective pharmacotherapy for PSC has not been established, and current educational reviews emphasize that no medical therapy has been shown to alter disease progression. Therefore, treatment should be directed at symptoms, bacterial cholangitis, biliary obstruction, portal-hypertensive and cirrhotic complications, nutritional consequences of cholestasis when present, and transplant candidacy. [13][19][21]

Endoscopic intervention is most relevant when a clinically significant biliary stricture is suspected because of worsening cholestasis, jaundice, pruritus, cholangitis, or concern for malignancy. ERCP can define the lesion, facilitate directed diagnostic assessment, and permit nonoperative dilation of dominant strictures. [11][22]

Refer patients with advanced disease to a transplant center before a crisis-driven evaluation. In addition to decompensated cirrhosis, recognized PSC-specific reasons to consider transplantation include recurrent bacterial cholangitis, intractable pruritus, severe jaundice, and high-grade biliary dysplasia. [16][21]
bullets: Offer clinical-trial consideration when feasible because investigational therapies remain important in a disease without proven disease-modifying medical treatment. [19]

Avoid labeling bile acid agents or immunosuppressive therapy as standard PSC treatment on the basis of the supplied evidence; no source provided supports a specific dose, efficacy threshold, or routine disease-modifying regimen.

In patients with suspected PSC-autoimmune hepatitis overlap or another competing immune-mediated liver disease, pursue disease-specific diagnostic clarification rather than treating typical large-duct PSC empirically as autoimmune hepatitis. [20][24]

subsections.heading: Transplant and cancer-directed pathways
paragraphs: Liver transplantation is the only curative therapy for advanced PSC in the supplied evidence. For selected hilar cholangiocarcinoma, U.S. transplantation may be considered when tumor diameter is less than 3 cm, there is no lymph-node or distant metastasis, and chemoradiotherapy has been given. [16][19]
bullets: Multidisciplinary assessment is essential when imaging or endoscopic evaluation raises concern for cholangiocarcinoma because resection, oncologic therapy, and transplant eligibility are stage-dependent. [16][23]

These are PSC-specific transplant considerations even without conventional decompensation alone. [16][21]

sections.heading: Surveillance should integrate biliary cancer and colonic risk
sections.intro: PSC follow-up should be structured around changing symptoms, cholestatic tests, biliary imaging findings, and IBD status.
paragraphs: Surveillance is justified by the substantial risk of cholangiocarcinoma and increased gallbladder cancer risk, but the supplied sources do not provide a single U.S. society-endorsed interval or a fully specified surveillance protocol. MRI/MRCP is central to evaluating concerning strictures or masses, and CA 19-9 is best interpreted as an adjunct because isolated elevation lacks sufficient specificity. [23]

Colonoscopy at PSC diagnosis is important to identify occult IBD. Continued colorectal cancer prevention should then be coordinated with gastroenterology using the patient’s IBD phenotype and current guideline-based surveillance plan; exact U.S. surveillance intervals are not supplied in the source set. [21]

At each follow-up, reassess for symptoms that indicate obstruction, infection, cancer, or hepatic decompensation: jaundice, escalating pruritus, fever or recurrent cholangitis, abdominal pain, weight loss, ascites, variceal bleeding, or encephalopathy. These changes should prompt expedited diagnostic reassessment rather than routine observation. [12][16][21][23]
bullets: Document whether IBD is present and coordinate hepatology-gastroenterology care; PSC-associated IBD can be clinically silent at liver diagnosis. [21]
Interpret a rising or elevated CA 19-9 in clinical context and alongside imaging, not as a stand-alone cancer diagnosis. [23]
Use transplant referral proactively for recurrent cholangitis, severe pruritus or jaundice, high-grade biliary dysplasia, or decompensated cirrhosis. [16][21]

May indicate obstruction, a relevant stricture, or malignancy [11][23]
Obtain prompt biliary reassessment; consider ERCP based on imaging and clinical findings. [11]

False-positive elevation is common in PSC [23]

faq.question: Is ERCP required to diagnose primary sclerosing cholangitis?
faq.answer: No. MRCP is generally the preferred initial cholangiographic study because it is noninvasive and visualizes ducts proximal to severe stenoses. Reserve ERCP for nondiagnostic MRCP with persistent suspicion or when a stricture needs diagnostic or therapeutic endoscopic assessment. [11]

faq.question: Should all patients with PSC undergo colonoscopy?
faq.answer: Patients without known IBD should undergo diagnostic colonoscopy because PSC frequently coexists with IBD; AASLD educational material cites an approximately 68% prevalence, predominantly ulcerative colitis. [21]

faq.question: Does an elevated CA 19-9 diagnose cholangiocarcinoma in PSC?
faq.answer: No. Up to 33% of patients with PSC may have elevated CA 19-9 without cholangiocarcinoma or another identified cause. Use it only as an adjunct to imaging and clinical evaluation of a suspicious stricture or mass. [23]

faq.question: What are PSC-specific indications for liver transplantation?
faq.answer: In addition to decompensated cirrhosis, transplantation may be considered for recurrent bacterial cholangitis, severe refractory pruritus or jaundice, high-grade biliary dysplasia, and selected cases of hilar cholangiocarcinoma. [16][21]
